title: Reranking, the highest-leverage upgrade
summary: Reranking is a sort step dropped in between retrieval and the model. Your first stage sets the ceiling and the reranker decides how much of it you collect. Measured on this course's lessons, the recall curve flattens at 15 candidates, so retrieving 50 would cost three times as much and buy nothing.
html:
Yesterday ended on two measured numbers: the cheap retriever put the right lesson first 30 percent of the time and somewhere in the top five 90 percent of the time. Today is how you collect the difference, and why this is the first thing to try when a RAG system gives mediocre answers.

What you actually build

Your retriever returns 50 candidates instead of 5. You send 50 pairs of query and document to a cross-encoder. It gives you back 50 numbers. You sort by those numbers, keep the top 5, and those 5 go into the prompt.

That is the whole change. A sort step inserted between retrieval and generation. Your index does not change. Your embeddings do not change. Your chunking does not change. You can put it behind a flag and turn it off.

Compare that to the alternatives for improving answer quality: re-chunking means reindexing everything, switching embedding models means reindexing everything, fine tuning means a training pipeline you do not have. Reranking is the only upgrade on the list that is purely additive, which is most of why it is the first one to reach for.

The one idea worth holding

The first stage sets the ceiling. The reranker decides how much of the ceiling you collect.

Put numbers on that. Say you retrieve 50 and keep 5, and suppose the right chunk is somewhere in those 50 for 95 out of 100 queries, but in the top 5 for only 60. Then:

95%   the ceiling: the reranker can never do better,
      because it can only reorder what it was given
60%   the floor: what you get with no reranker at all
35%   the headroom a reranker is competing for

Everything about tuning a cascade comes out of that picture. If the ceiling is low, a reranker cannot save you and you have a retrieval problem. If the floor is already close to the ceiling, a reranker buys you very little and you are paying latency for nothing.

The analogy: the retriever is a junior who brings you fifty folders from the archive, and the reranker is the senior who flips through them and hands you the five worth reading. The senior cannot help with a folder the junior left in the archive.

The two knobs

There are only two. How many you retrieve, and how many survive into the prompt.

Retrieve-k sets the ceiling and sets the cost. Cost is linear: at roughly a millisecond per pair, 20 candidates is 20 milliseconds and 200 candidates is 200 milliseconds. There is no cleverness available here, you just pay.

Keep-n sets what the model sees. People get this one wrong in a specific way: they retrieve 100, rerank beautifully, and then put 20 chunks in the prompt, which puts the junk straight back in. If your reranker works, keeping fewer is better. Day 55 is about what long contexts do to a model's attention, and it is the reason keep-n is usually 3 to 8 rather than 20.

If you want to see it measured

Same setup as yesterday, now over 37 lessons: ten questions I labelled with the lesson that answers each, ranked by BM25. Here is the full recall curve, which is the ceiling as a function of retrieve-k.

retrieve-k    ceiling
     1          30%
     2          50%
     3          60%
     5          90%
     8          90%
    10          90%
    15         100%
    20         100%

Read where it flattens. The curve climbs steeply to 5, sits flat from 5 to 10, reaches everything by 15, and after that retrieving more is pure cost. If I sized this cascade by instinct I would have retrieved 50, paid three times the reranking latency, and gained exactly nothing over 15.

That is the measurement worth copying. Not my numbers, which come from ten queries over 37 documents and are far too easy to be a benchmark. The method: label some queries, plot where the right answer sits, and set retrieve-k at the knee of that curve rather than at a round number somebody put in a blog post.

Where reranking does not help

Three honest limits.

It cannot find what retrieval missed. If your recall at 100 candidates is 40 percent, a perfect reranker gives you 40 percent. Adding a reranker to cover for bad chunking is the most common misuse, and it hides the real problem behind a plausible looking improvement.

It puts a model call on the critical path. Every query now depends on it. With a hosted reranking API that is a network hop and an outside dependency with its own bad days.

It may not transfer to your corpus. Off the shelf rerankers are trained mostly on web search relevance data. On legal text, internal jargon or code, I think the gains are routinely oversold, and I have seen the claim that they can be negative. That is my read rather than a settled result, and the only way to know is to measure it on your own labelled queries. Which is the same advice as the paragraph above, because it is always the same advice.

If you remember one thing
Your retriever sets the ceiling, the reranker collects what it can of it. Measure the recall curve, put retrieve-k at the knee, and keep fewer chunks than feels comfortable.

Tomorrow: wiring this into an actual cascade, where the stages have to agree on what they are passing each other.
exercise:
One. Write your day 38 note.

Two. Sketch the recall curve for a retriever you have access to, even roughly. Pick five questions you know the answer document for, run them, and write down the rank of the right document each time. Five numbers is enough to see whether your knee is at 10, at 50, or nowhere yet. If the right document is missing entirely for two of the five, you have learned something more useful than any reranker would have told you.
